subject: Architecture
title: Hagia Sophia: The Dome That Changed Everything
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hagia Sophia: The Dome That Changed Everything.

hook.text: Emperor Justinian wanted a building so grand it would make Solomon jealous.

buildup.text: In just five years, 10,000 workers built a dome 180 feet high with no internal supports.

discovery.text: Forty windows ring the dome's base, making it appear to float on a ring of light.

twist.text: The dome collapsed in an earthquake 21 years after completion and had to be rebuilt higher.

climax.text: Hagia Sophia served as a church, a mosque, and a museum — all within the same walls.

punchline.text: One building. Three religions. Fifteen hundred years of awe.

quiz.question: What creates the illusion of the Hagia Sophia dome floating?
options: Mirror tiles reflecting the interior light
Forty windows ringing the dome's base
A thin cable system suspending it from above

details.summary: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, completed in 537 CE under Emperor Justinian, features a 31-meter dome that appears to float on a ring of 40 windows. Its innovative pendentive system — triangular curved sections transferring a round dome to a square base — became the standard for domed construction.
details.whyItMatters: Hagia Sophia solved the fundamental problem of placing a circular dome on a square room. Its pendentive technology spread across Islamic and Christian architecture, enabling the great domed mosques and cathedrals built for the next 1,500 years.
takeaways: 31-meter dome appears to float on a ring of 40 windows
Pendentive system transfers circular dome to square base
This technology enabled domed construction for 1,500 years

faq.question: What are pendentives?
faq.answer: Pendentives are curved triangular surfaces that transition between a circular dome and the square plan below. They fill the corners between the arches that support the dome, creating a smooth curved surface.

faq.question: Has Hagia Sophia's dome ever collapsed?
faq.answer: The original dome partially collapsed in 558 CE after an earthquake. It was rebuilt higher and with reinforced ribs. Further repairs followed after earthquakes in 989 and 1346. Massive buttresses added over centuries help stabilize the structure.
